subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Note for Aditi's parents, from her violin teacher. Aditi arrived early and played the opening piece from last term, the one she has known by heart since March. She played it three times, smiling each time, and asked if she could play it again. When I turned to the new page with the fast finger shifts, she said her hand was tired. So I asked her to play only the four hard bars, slowly, five times, and we marked each try with a pencil tick. By the fifth try the notes were cleaner. She frowned but stayed. Please let her start home practice with those four bars. Damini, music teacher

qa.q: How many times did Aditi play the old piece when she arrived?
qa.a: She played it three times, smiling each time.

qa.q: What might Aditi be feeling when she says her hand is tired at the new page?
qa.a: She is probably uneasy or discouraged. The old piece feels good and the new page is hard, so a tired hand may be a way to avoid the difficult part.

qa.q: What small step could Aditi's parents take to help at home?
qa.a: They could ask her to play the four hard bars slowly at the start of practice, before the piece she already knows.

qa.q: How does Damini see Aditi's repeated playing of the old piece?
qa.a: Damini sees it as enjoyable but not much practice, which is why the teacher moved her to the hard bars and marked each try.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a mastered violin piece because it feels good while the difficult bars are where growth lives.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Tuesday evening. Played my favourite keyboard tune again, the rain song. Six times! It feels so nice when my fingers already know where to go. Deepika didi came in and listened and said it sounded lovely, then asked why I never play the second page. I said it's boring and I get it wrong. She said the wrong bit is where fingers learn. She showed me just two bars, left hand only, very slowly. I got them wrong seven times and I was cross. Then once right. Tomorrow I will do the two bars before the rain song, not after. Leela

qa.q: How many times did Leela play the rain song?
qa.a: Leela played the rain song six times.

qa.q: Why was Leela cross while practising the two bars?
qa.a: Leela felt frustrated because getting the two bars wrong seven times felt worse than the easy tune that always goes right. 😕

qa.q: What choice did Leela make for the next day's practice?
qa.a: Leela decided to play the two bars before the rain song instead of after, so the hard part comes first.

qa.q: How does Deepika see the wrong notes Leela plays?
qa.a: Deepika treats the wrong notes as the place where fingers learn, so the second page is worth the effort.

grounding: Shows a child replaying an already easy tune for pleasure and only later working on the hard bars.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Every evening after school, Abhinav, ten, sat on the mango-tree platform outside his house in the village and played his bamboo flute. He always played the same folk tune, the one he'd learned first. It came out smooth and sweet, and the neighbours clapped. His teacher, Vinita didi, had given him a new piece with fast notes in the middle. He tried it once, squeaked, and went back to the old tune. For a month this went on. At the Holi gathering, Vinita didi asked him to play the new piece. He stumbled at the fast part and stopped, red-faced. Walking home, he said, "But I practised every day." She smiled gently. "You practised the easy part every day."

qa.q: Where did Abhinav play his flute every evening?
qa.a: He played on the mango-tree platform outside his house.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav keep going back to the old tune?
qa.a: Playing it felt good and sounded sweet, while the new piece made him squeak and feel embarrassed.

qa.q: What could Abhinav do in his evening practice from now on?
qa.a: Spend most of the time on the fast notes in the new piece, slowly at first, and play the old tune only at the end as a treat.

qa.q: How does Vinita didi see Abhinav's month of practice?
qa.a: Vinita didi sees that he practised only what was already easy, and gently points it out.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps repeating a tune he has mastered because it feels good, while the hard new piece does not grow.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: Omar, eleven, lived in Amman and wanted to be the school team's striker. Every afternoon in the courtyard he took shots with his right foot, the strong one, from the same spot. Bang, bang, bang, into the net. It felt great. His older sister Rania watched from the balcony. "Why don't you ever use your left?" "It's bad," he said. "The ball goes everywhere." At the trial, the coach sent crosses to his left side. Omar missed four of five. That evening Rania came down with a bag of old balls. "Twenty left-foot shots first. Then you can do your fancy right ones." Omar grumbled, but set the first ball down on his left.

qa.q: Which foot did Omar always use in the courtyard?
qa.a: He took shots with his right foot, the strong one.

qa.q: How did Omar feel about shooting with his left foot?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and discouraged, because the ball went everywhere, so he avoided it.

qa.q: What did Rania suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Twenty left-foot shots before the right-foot ones, so practice goes to the weak part where growth is possible.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt watching the trial go badly?
qa.a: Rania likely felt sorry for her brother but also sure that the easy practice was the problem, so she came down to help.

grounding: Shows a child repeating the shots he already does well because it feels good, until a trial shows the gap.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage: At the Saturday music school, Simran, nine, sat at the keyboard in practice room three. Her teacher Swati ma'am had asked her to work on the new scale with the thumb crossing. Instead Simran played "Twinkle Twinkle" with both hands, beautifully, again and again, humming along. When Swati ma'am looked in after twenty minutes, Simran beamed. "I practised!" "What did you practise?" Simran's smile flickered. "Twinkle." Swati ma'am sat beside her. "You play that perfectly. That's why it feels nice. The scale feels bad because you're still learning it. That's where the growing happens." She set a timer: ten minutes scale, then one Twinkle as a reward.

qa.q: Which practice room was Simran in?
qa.a: Simran was in practice room three.

qa.q: What did Simran's smile flickering suggest?
qa.a: It suggested she felt a little caught out and uneasy, realising she hadn't practised the scale she was asked to learn.

qa.q: How did Swati ma'am help, and why might it work?
qa.a: She explained why the easy piece feels good and the scale feels bad, then set ten minutes of scale with one Twinkle as a reward.

qa.q: How might Swati ma'am feel on seeing Simran play Twinkle again?
qa.a: She might feel amused and understanding, since enjoying a mastered piece is natural, but she knows it isn't where Simran will grow.

grounding: Shows a child repeating a mastered piece because it feels good, and a teacher steering her to the harder part.

subtopic: Learning a craft by deliberate practice
passage:
Saturday: At the colony skating rink, Usha glided round and round, arms out, grinning. Forward laps were her favourite; the wheels hummed. "Usha, T-stop drill, please!" called Sachin, the coach. She did one wobbly try, then went back to her laps. "I'm practising," she said.
Next Saturday: Sachin blew the whistle for the relay. Usha raced forward beautifully and then could not stop at the cone. She slammed into the rail and sat down hard, cheeks burning. The others had stopped neatly.
Wednesday: Usha asked to come early. For twenty minutes she did nothing but T-stops, one foot dragging behind. She fell twice and muttered, "This is boring and horrible." Sachin counted each try with her. On the last one she stopped on the line, and her mouth fell open.

qa.q: What did Usha do when Sachin called for the T-stop drill on the first Saturday?
qa.a: She did one wobbly try, then went back to her laps.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling after slamming into the rail?
qa.a: Usha was embarrassed and upset; her cheeks were burning while the others had stopped neatly.

qa.q: What could Usha keep doing in every session?
qa.a: Spend part of each session on the hard drill, like the twenty minutes of T-stops, before the fun forward laps.

qa.q: How might Sachin feel watching Usha stop on the line on Wednesday?
qa.a: Sachin is probably pleased and proud, having counted every try with Usha and watched the boring drill finally pay off.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps repeating the easy, enjoyable part of skating, and improves only after working on the hard part.
